stage_description: The hatchling stage covers roughly the first 5% of a reptile's life, but the calendar age varies enormously by species: a leopard gecko lives about 15–20 years, while a box turtle can exceed 40, so a hatchling may be only weeks or several months old. Correct husbandry is the single most important factor at this fragile stage. Newly hatched reptiles are highly sensitive to a wrong temperature gradient, incorrect UVB, or the wrong humidity, and most early losses trace back to husbandry errors rather than disease. Set up a species-appropriate enclosure with a warm basking spot and a cooler end, several hides, and (for many species) shallow water for soaking, and check every parameter against a care sheet for your exact species.
nutrition: Feeding depends entirely on the species: carnivorous hatchlings such as many snakes and geckos take appropriately small prey, insectivores eat small feeder insects, and herbivores or omnivores such as many tortoises and some lizards need finely chopped greens and vegetables. Growing hatchlings feed more often than adults. Dust insects with calcium, often together with vitamin D3, as recommended for your species to support rapid bone growth and prevent metabolic bone disease.
activity: Provide a properly sized enclosure with a clear temperature gradient, a basking zone, correct UVB for diurnal species, and several secure hides so a nervous hatchling feels safe. Enrichment means natural furnishings: branches, cork bark, plants, and species-appropriate chances to climb or dig, plus a shallow water dish for soaking in many species. Keep handling brief and gentle while the animal settles into its new home.
veterinary_check_frequency: Book a first visit with a reptile or exotics veterinarian soon after acquiring a hatchling to confirm the species, the sex where possible, and a healthy start, and consider a fecal test for parasites. For a healthy youngster an annual wellness exam is a reasonable baseline, with husbandry reviewed at every visit.
dental_care: Most reptiles do not have brushable teeth, so oral care mainly means watching the mouth for infectious stomatitis (mouth rot): redness, swelling, drooling, or cheesy material around the jaw. Correct food and good husbandry are the best prevention, and any mouth abnormality warrants a reptile vet.
warning_signs: Contact a reptile vet if a hatchling is lethargic, refuses food for an unusual period, shows a swollen or soft jaw, breathes with an open mouth or makes wheezing or mucous sounds, or has retained shed on the toes, tail, or eyes. Sunken eyes, wrinkled skin from dehydration, and soft or deformed bones also need prompt attention.
